newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africans want amnesty for murder of U.S. woman.
newsitem.headline: S.Africans want amnesty for murder of U.S. woman.

text.p: Four black youths who murdered white American student Amy Biehl in a township attack four years ago are appealing for amnesty for the crime, South Africa's "truth commission" said on Friday.
Biehl, a 26-year-old Fulbright scholar, was stoned, stabbed and battered to death by a mob as she drove friends home in Cape Town's Guguletu township in August 1993.

Her family, from Newport Beach, California, will attend an amnesty hearing on July 8 for the four murderers currently serving 18-year jail terms, the Truth and Reconciliation Commission said in a statement.
The judges who presided at the killers' trials found Biehl was killed simply because she was white.
The murderers said they were supporters of the black radical Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), which has told the commission that its members targeted whites in the fight against apartheid.
The commission, set up to probe human rights abuses in the fight over apartheid, faces court action from the party which ruled South Africa in the years of enforced racial separation.
The white-dominated National Party, which is now in opposition, began a court action on Friday to gag criticism of it by commission chairman Archbishop Desmond Tutu and to force his deputy to quit.

The party, which implemented apartheid in 1948, lodged an urgent application in the Cape Town high court for an order finding that Tutu had violated the requirement for impartiality in the legislation setting up the commission.

The application cites comments by Tutu and his deputy Alex Boraine at a news conference last month when they criticised National Party leader F.W. de Klerk for not accepting the view his party's policy caused gross human rights violations during apartheid.

The National Party has boycotted the commission since then, accusing it of being biased in favour of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress, which took power in South Africa's first all-race elections in 1994.
Influential independent political analysts have expressed support for the National Party position that Tutu has failed to take a neutral political stance.
The party's court application, to be heard on August 26, seeks an order directing Tutu "to refrain... from compromising his impartiality or harming the credibility of the (commission)".
It asks that Boraine be ordered to quit and that the commission "refrain from making public statements which reasonably convey the impression that any issue before it may have been prejudged".
A separate National Party statement rejected a call from the commission, issued on Thursday, for urgent talks to resolve their differences.
The party has said that the comments by Tutu and Boraine in May effectively found it guilty of atrocities during the apartheid era.
